summary: Parag turns milk into products such as Gowardhan ghee and paneer, Go cheese, Pride of Cows dairy, Topp Up milk drinks and Avvatar products made using the liquid left from cheese-making.
description: The company arranges milk supply, checks it and processes it into products people can buy. Making cheese, selling fresh milk and supplying a restaurant with dairy ingredients need different equipment, storage and delivery arrangements.
money: Households and business buyers pay for dairy products or ingredients. Parag pays for milk, processing, packaging, storage, transport, staff and advertising. Selling a premium product can bring a higher price, but producing and delivering it may also cost more.
customers: Shoppers buy dairy products through shops and other sales channels. Restaurants and other food businesses buy products or ingredients in formats suited to their kitchens. Some customers receive dairy through direct home delivery.
drivers: The cost and quality of milk, how much of each product sells, keeping products fresh, reliable delivery and how much money is tied up in unsold stock or unpaid bills.

groups.title: Everyday dairy for the home
groups.examples: Gowardhan milk, ghee, paneer, curd and butter.
groups.explanation: Think of buying ghee for cooking or paneer for a meal. The company must buy suitable milk, make and pack the product, and get it to the customer before its usable life ends.

groups.title: Cheese and other products for homes and kitchens
groups.examples: Go cheese, cream and related dairy products.
groups.explanation: A household may buy a small cheese pack while a restaurant needs a larger supply for repeated use. Packaging, prices and delivery arrangements can differ even when the products come from the same dairy process.

groups.title: Home-delivered dairy and milk drinks
groups.examples: Pride of Cows offerings and Topp Up flavoured milk.
groups.explanation: Supplying dairy directly to homes requires regular deliveries. Packaged milk drinks follow their own storage instructions and sales routes; do not assume every milk product needs the same handling.

groups.title: Products made using whey
groups.examples: Avvatar whey-based products and related ingredients.
groups.explanation: Whey is the liquid left when milk is separated to make cheese. Processing it can create another product to sell. Turning it into a packaged brand still requires equipment, quality checks and paying customers; the brand name alone does not establish a health benefit.

basics.title: The same milk can produce several useful outputs
basics.text: Milk contains fat and other components. Processing can separate them for products such as cheese, cream and whey. The company needs to find useful buyers for the outputs, not just sell the most recognisable brand.

basics.title: Storage time is a business issue
basics.text: Products have different usable lives and storage needs. A fresh product that is not sold in time can be wasted. Products kept longer still use storage space, electricity and money that cannot yet be used elsewhere.

steps.title: Arrange and check milk supply
steps.text: Buy milk and check its quality before processing. Supply and cost can change with the season.

steps.title: Make the products
steps.text: Process milk into the required dairy products and ingredients, controlling quality and using the different outputs.

steps.title: Pack, store and deliver
steps.text: Choose packaging and storage appropriate to each product, then send it to shops, business buyers or homes.

steps.title: Collect payment and buy the next supply
steps.text: Receive payment under the sales terms while continuing to pay for milk, staff, transport and other running costs.

specifics.title: Milk can become dearer before pack prices change
specifics.text: Parag may have to pay more for milk while selling products at the previous price. The effect depends on which products it sells and whether it can change prices without losing too many customers.

specifics.title: Cheese and whey are linked
specifics.text: Making cheese also produces whey. Selling both can make better use of the milk, but the company still has to cover the equipment, processing, storage and selling costs involved.

specifics.title: A full warehouse is not the same as a successful sale
specifics.text: Stock is product waiting to be sold. It uses money and may lose value if demand or market prices fall. Customer bills that remain unpaid also leave less cash for the next milk purchase.

watch: Is enough suitable milk available at a workable price?
Milk is the starting input for the dairy products.
Read supply and milk-cost commentary alongside changes in product prices. Check whether the company is paying more for milk before it can recover that increase from customers.
Which products and buyers are increasing sales?
More cheese sold to restaurants is different from a higher price on a home pack.
Read sales commentary for everyday dairy, cheese, drinks and whey products. Separate changes in quantities from changes in price, and household demand from business-customer demand.
Are the factories producing goods that buyers want?
New equipment does not earn money just because it can run.
Look for actual production, demand and use of the installed equipment. Check whether cheese and other outputs can be sold together and whether processing or storage limits hold up sales.
Is product moving out before it loses value?
Unsold dairy and unpaid customer bills tie up money.

Compare stock, expiry or write-off disclosures, customer balances and cash from running the business. Ask whether stock is being held for a clear seasonal need or because sales are slower than expected.
Do quality and delivery support repeat buying?
A familiar brand still needs safe products and reliable availability.

Read quality, returns, storage and delivery disclosures. Check whether wider distribution needs extra refrigeration, transport, advertising or credit to shops, rather than assuming a premium price means a higher profit.
risks: Milk supply becomes costly or unreliable
The company may struggle to obtain suitable milk or recover higher costs through selling prices.
Products spoil or fail quality checks
Poor handling, storage or production problems can cause waste, recalls or lost trust.
Stock sells for less than expected
Weak demand or changing dairy-product prices can reduce what stored products are worth.
Expansion uses cash before sales follow
Factories, delivery routes and new brands need money before they generate enough customer payments.
context: A supermarket pack and a restaurant supply have different journeys

A household buys a convenient pack; a restaurant may order a larger amount repeatedly. Compare the packing, delivery and payment terms instead of treating all dairy sales as the same kind of business.
quiz: Does a higher-priced dairy pack automatically leave more profit?
No. Milk, processing, packaging, storage, transport and advertising may cost more too. The price has to be compared with the costs of supplying that product.
sources: Historical processing background: cheese and whey

financialNotes.title: Verify scope before reading brand economics
financialNotes.text: The table uses audited consolidated operating revenue and statutory profit after tax, including the reported exceptional provision. The group reports a milk-related operating segment; familiar dairy brands and product categories do not each have a separately disclosed profit. Marketing claims are not a replacement for the signed accounts.

financialNotes.title: Read the balance sheet with the income statement
financialNotes.text: Inventory, receivables, borrowing and investment can explain why a growing dairy business requires cash. A profit figure alone does not show how much remains after processing expansion and stock needs.
